episodes.title: What Will Determine the Durability of the AI Investment Cycle?
episodes.summary:
**Summary**
Goldman Sachs' Allison Nathan discusses the durability of the AI investment cycle with Social Capital's Chamath Palihapitiya and GS analyst Eric Sheridan, following recent AI-related stress in equity and credit markets and post-midterm regulatory uncertainty. The debate centers on whether hyperscaler AI capex will generate adequate ROI before investor patience runs out — a key swing factor for broad risk sentiment and credit spreads.

**Key points**
- Palihapitiya flags NeoClouds (AI infrastructure financiers) as structurally mismatched: short-dated, speculative revenue against long-dated, fixed obligations, likened to airlines needing 80-85% utilization to break even versus current ~70-75%.
- Credit markets have already "sniffed out" the risk — spreads and CDS on NeoCloud-related debt have widened.
- Binding constraint has shifted from chips to power/land; actual AI ROI remains elusive despite surging token/agent consumption — EPS gains are rarely attributable to AI versus buybacks or pricing power.
- Sheridan notes hyperscalers (Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet, Meta) have shown credible ROIC and backlog conversion, and would need only ~50% of backlog monetized to clear a 15%+ return hurdle; memory-price inflation is a cost surprise.
- Both agree hyperscalers (pristine balance sheets, cash flow) are insulated; risk is concentrated in NeoClouds and non-hyperscaler AI-levered names trading at depressed single/low-double-digit EPS multiples.

**FX / rates implications**
- Primarily a US tech/credit-market story; limited direct EM read-through, but a disorderly AI-credit unwind (NeoCloud defaults, spread widening) would be a classic risk-off trigger — pressuring EM Asia and LATAM FX (INR, IDR, MXN, BRL) via global risk appetite and credit-spread contagion channels, and could pull UST yields lower on flight-to-quality.
- Continued hyperscaler capex/equity resilience would keep broader risk sentiment supportive for carry trades.

**Watch list**
- NeoCloud utilization rates and CDS/credit spreads as an early-warning signal.
- Hyperscaler capex guidance and ROIC disclosures in upcoming earnings (following Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet, Meta commentary already cited).
- Power/land supply constraints and any further equity/credit drawdowns tied to the AI theme into 2027-2028.

episodes.title: MacroVoices #560 Daniel Lacalle: “The European ER AH Situation…”
episodes.summary:
**Summary**
Daniel Lacalle (Tressis) joins MacroVoices to dissect last week's market bloodbath, arguing the AI CapEx story isn't a bubble but needs earnings clarity, while US dollar strength reflects a "least bad alternative" dynamic against a euro area facing stagnation and redenomination risk. The market desk segment adds tactical levels across S&P 500, gold, oil, copper and Treasuries that drive the cross-asset risk sentiment feeding into EM.

**Key points**
- DXY testing ~104 resistance on Fed hawkishness and flight-to-safety demand rather than fundamentals; Lacalle doubts further aggressive dollar appreciation given the systemic risk an overpriced dollar poses (prior Asian/LatAm crises cited).
- Fed criticized for over-relying on rate hikes vs. balance-sheet/liquidity tools, hitting financial conditions hard with limited actual inflation impact.
- US, China and Russia reportedly cooperating on refined-product supply security amid Iran/Ukraine conflicts; WTI seen settling near $68-70; European nat gas to stay structurally elevated vs US prices.
- Euro area described as carrying "redenomination risk" from fiscal stagnation despite ECB negative rates and stimulus; France/Italy euro-exit seen as near-impossible due to TARGET2 imbalances, but a more debased euro is the likely endgame.
- Gold fell sharply (implied vol jumped from 22% to 34%) but Lacalle calls it a buying opportunity given tight physical supply and central-bank demand; desk flags 3,300 as key support, with 2025's 3,300 consolidation zone as the deeper retest level.
- Market desk: S&P 6900 is the level to hold or risk a drop to 6400-6500; copper down over 20% in a month back to March lows; UST 10y fell from 535bp to 485bp, signaling AI-capex growth concerns and raising odds the Fed pauses hikes in December.
- Mexico, North Africa and parts of Latin America flagged as likely beneficiaries if US data-center buildout is constrained by local moratoriums, given their spare power-generation capacity.

**FX / rates implications**
- Sustained DXY strength paired with a hawkish-but-conflicted Fed is the key transmission channel into EM Asia/LATAM funding costs and carry; any Fed pivot signal (flagged for the December FOMC) would be a key EM FX relief catalyst.
- Euro-debasement thesis and French/Italian fiscal stress support continued EUR weakness, a broad risk-off cross-current for EM FX via dollar strength.
- Oil/gold/copper setups (asymmetric upside in oil, gold pullback framed as a buying opportunity, oversold copper) matter for commodity-linked EM currencies (BRL, CLP, COP, MXN) and broader risk sentiment.
- Potential for AI-driven data-center investment to redirect toward Mexico/Latin America/North Africa is a tail flow consideration for those economies if US politics blocks domestic buildout.

**Watch list**
- December FOMC meeting: further hikes vs. a pause signal given tightening financial conditions.
- S&P 500 6900 support — a break risks a retest of 6400-6500.
- Gold support at 3,300; DXY resistance at 104.
- Iran/Ukraine refinery-strike risk to the US-China-Russia energy supply agreement.

episodes.title: America's spending paradox
episodes.summary:
**Summary**
University of Michigan Surveys of Consumers director Joanne Hsu discusses November's uptick in US consumer sentiment and the widening gap between gloomy sentiment readings and resilient consumer spending. The divergence matters for macro traders because it complicates reading US consumer strength off spending data alone, and because the survey's inflation-expectations series is closely watched by the Fed as a policy input.

**Key points**
- November sentiment rose slightly on falling gas prices, post-midterm election relief (consumers shifted left, expecting divided government to slow policy), and despite continued stock market turbulence.
- Sentiment hit a record low in May 2025 and second-lowest reading in October 2025 despite resilient GDP growth and a strong labor market.
- Consumer spending (~70% of GDP) is increasingly driven by wealthy, asset-rich households benefiting from high stock and home valuations; lower-income consumers are financing spending via borrowing/dissaving as pandemic-era savings are exhausted.
- Inflation expectations fell sharply from October to November (election, falling gas) but remain above pre-Iran-war and 2024 levels.
- Tariff fears from early 2025 did not fully materialize; consumers revised inflation expectations down quickly once realized tariffs came in lower than initially announced.
- A growing share of consumers (a November surge) spontaneously cite AI-bubble concerns, though this remains a distant third concern behind tariffs/high prices and gas prices.
- Only ~10-11% of consumers expect income gains to outstrip inflation next year, down from ~20% eighteen months ago — a historically low share.
- Rising 2026 healthcare costs are flagged as a likely offset to any energy-price relief.

**FX / rates implications**
- Soft/mixed US consumer signals and sticky-but-falling inflation expectations feed into Fed policy expectations, with knock-on effects for UST yields, DXY and broad EM risk appetite/carry trades.
- Growing AI-bubble anxiety among wealthier, equity-exposed US consumers is a risk-sentiment indicator worth tracking; a sharp equity drawdown would hit the wealth-driven spending channel supporting US growth and could trigger a broader risk-off move pressuring EM FX.
- Inflation expectations tied partly to Iran-related gas price moves link oil risk premia to US consumer psychology and, indirectly, to the Fed's reaction function.

**Watch list**
- Next University of Michigan sentiment and inflation-expectations releases for signs of re-acceleration if gas prices or Iran-related geopolitical risk flares again.
- 2026 healthcare cost increases as a potential drag on US consumer purchasing power and spending next year.
- Any further deterioration in labor-market expectations, which have so far stayed stable versus 2025's tariff-driven scare.
